abstract: The SCALE Initiative at the Stanford Graduate School of Education conducted a rigorous evidence review of the empirical literature on AI in K-12 education. Reviewing more than 800 academic papers (now over 1,100 in the underlying repository), the team identified only 20 studies that met high-quality causal standards for measuring how AI tools actually affect students or educators. The review argues that adoption is outpacing evidence, and that many popular claims about AI in classrooms rest on weak causal foundations.
keyFindings: Reviewed more than 800 academic papers related to AI and K-12 education; underlying research repository now over 1,100 papers
Only 20 high-quality causal studies were identified as rigorously examining how AI tools affect student or educator outcomes
'Student performance often improves with access to AI tools, but once removed, results are mixed'
'No high-quality causal studies of student AI use conducted in U.S. K-12 classrooms' were found among the reviewed literature
AI tools designed with pedagogical guardrails show more promising outcomes than general-purpose chatbots
Widening gap between K-12 AI adoption and the causal-evidence base to justify it
methodology: Systematic review of the academic literature on AI in K-12 education. Papers were screened against a strict causal-inference bar: 'studies that convincingly estimate causal impact, meaning studies that can tell us whether an AI tool changed outcomes.' The review distinguishes between correlational, descriptive, and causal studies, and separately assesses performance with AI access (during the task) versus without AI access (post-tool retention).
qualifiers: The review does not directly measure workforce displacement — its scope is student and educator outcomes, not employment. Findings apply to K-12 specifically and may not generalize to higher education or non-classroom education workforce. The 'only 20 causal studies' framing is a rigor bar, not a claim that AI has no effect. The Stanford SCALE team is explicit that stronger causal evidence is needed before firm impact claims can be made.
